articles.title: Films and politics
articles.content: I HAPPENED to catch an Indian film on Netflix this week, Daayra. And for some reason, it stayed with me so much that I would rather write about it this week than any of the more important topics such as soobay, local governments, kruption and the various political statements on each of these issues. The film caught my eye because it starred Kareena Kapoor in a non-glam role, which in itself should have sent off alarm bells. The last such film she did was also rather meh but then film watching is generally a case of hope over experience. Or simply just boredom when it comes to streaming platforms. This too appeared to be an OTT release and revolved around police encounters; the second reason for my interest. After all, it’s an issue that has garnered much attention these days in Pakistan. The film revolves around a brutal gang rape and murder of a young woman and the police on the hunt for the accused. Once they are caught, the police team sent to catch them take a quick decision to kill them all in an encounter. And the encounter leads to what appears to be nationwide celebrations by ordinary people. The police officer who led the chase and the encounter becomes a celebrity who is asked for ‘selfies’ and why not, for his biceps are just as impressive and just as tightly clad as those of the spies in Dharundar. Storytelling has become more cautious in the Indian film industry, especially where politics is concerned. But despite the celebratory mood, some human rights organisations file petitions compelling the police to send an internal team to investigate the incident. Enter Kapoor and her band of police-wallahs. The rest of the film provides two parallel accounts of the rape and its investigation by the police team and the one by the internal affairs team. And somehow this is where the film loses its focus — perhaps it was meant to play out like a debate between why encounters happen in societies such as ours and why they shouldn’t. But either for lack of focus or beliefs, the script leans in favour of encounters to ensure ‘justice’ in a creaky system that is a punishment in itself. For example, there are ample references to the Delhi case culprits and that the system failed in ensuring closure. One of the Delhi rape case culprits even makes an appearance in the film; the juvenile who has now been settled elsewhere with a different identity. In another instance, the mother of the victim, when told of the arrests, contradicts the police officer who is trying to tell her that her suffering is over; for her it is about to begin with endless trips to the courts. The police officer and she are then united in their grief it seems — the grief of no quick and clear end. But the film just doesn’t play on the grief caused by lengthy court cases. It removes nuance altogether in its portrayal of the accused. They are working-class men who guzzle whisky in their downtime and then rape and murder women. This is their pastime and they have the routine down pat. Little effort is made to add any humanity to them — even the family of the main accused is quick to argue that he could barely talk and would get the benefit of reduced mental capacity. That a poor family is even aware of such concessions in the legal system is interesting. In contrast, the police officers are honest, hardworking men and women who simply want to help the victim’s family bring closure and rid the world of evil. There are no corrupt police officers here who carry out encounters at the behest of the powerful and/or end up targeting innocent people, out of sheer incompetence or for money. There are no politicians in this world who might be pushing this policy on the law enforcement personnel. It’s simply the police with hearts of gold, who are playing vigilantes, the way Amitabh was an angry young man, fighting against the system. There is little to counter all this. Just Kareena Kapoor and her vague belief in following procedure and trusting the system. The morality of the matter and the havoc it can wreak is left to the audience’s imagination and understanding. There is no mention of corruption or policemen or politicians who might turn encounters into a policy or the death of innocent people. Nor are there any rich or privileged accused who could perhaps not be disposed of this easily. There is little debate or grey areas here, despite the film’s pretensions. And no nuance or issue to explore; something that hits home here in Pakistan with our recent debates over extrajudicial killings in Punjab and elsewhere. Or the death of Naqeebullah which led to the rise of the PTM. It makes one wonder if the filmmaker, Meghna Gulzar, set out to indict the system over how it treats rapists, or the poor understanding and writing led to a less nuanced approach. Be that as it may, there is also the larger arc of the Indian film industry where storytelling has become more cautious, especially where political commentary is concerned. Meghna Gulzar’s father, filmmaker Gulzar, lived at a time when he could make films such as Maachis, which was a beautiful and nuanced account of the insurgency in Indian Punjab. Twenty years later, it is a film that continues to haunt viewers for its depiction of those who got caught in an insurgency. And while one can debate the skills of one filmmaker compared to another, it is perhaps also about the space available in a society for difficult conversations on politics and their depiction in different forms. Conversations that lead not just to understanding but also the depiction of issues in writing and on celluloid. This is an issue that plagues the neighbours on both sides of the border — we are still joined together in more ways than we realise.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: Being civil to begin with
articles.content: THAT Pakistan issending a ministerto attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi on Nov 20 should be applauded even if it’s not clear that this could be the proverbial ice breaker between the perpetually aloof neighbours. It is, however, worth hoping for. The agenda for a civilisational dialogue should be fun for the participants, although India’s decade-old Hindu revivalist government may drag its feet on the issue. Bilateral ties can still improve despite this handicap. Reports are circulating of cross-border trade also picking up — albeit discreetly — between India and Pakistan in recent days. Renowned political analyst Trita Parsi used a phrase to describe the options for a low-key US retreat from the war-torn Gulf region, which may be relevant for India-Pakistan ties. Parsi likened Donald Trump’s options for a face-saving pullout from his self-created mess to Swiss cheese. Sanctions on paper and holes inside, like the bubbles within a good Swiss cheese. The US could keep its formal sanctions on the books so the administration can publicly claim it is still maintaining pressure on Tehran. In reality, the enforcement is invisibly relaxed. Which is what might work, if nothing else does, for the South Asian neighbours — an unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities. Behind the scenes, in Parsi’s version of a workable Gulf resolution, the US gradually loosens its naval blockade and stops aggressively enforcing sanctions. This creates large “holes” in the economic pressure — much like the Swiss cheese — allowing Asian, Middle Eastern, and Gulf countries to resume trading with and investing in Iran without fear of US retaliation. At some opportune moment, even if the currently tense atmosphere results in another catastrophic flare-up, peace would be the only game in town, possibly giving credence to Trita Parsi’s face-saving device. The immediate trigger for the latest round of signalling, if it indeed adds up to some kind of undeclared rapprochement, springs from very practical and commonsensical exigencies that require all neighbours to collectively deal with the huge economic challenges dogging the world. The platform offered by the SCO has been used and abused by both sides in the past to launch verbal attacks on each other. Could the tide have turned? The agenda at hand for Dr Musadik Malik, Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, representing Pakistan at the meeting could present challenges as well as chances to resolve them. However, the larger theme of a civilisational dialogue that brings all SCO members together may have to confront some predictable handwringing from India. An unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities could work for South Asia. The idea of civilisation imagines a palpable and unbroken link between the past and the present. In its understanding of India’s past, however, the Hindutva establishment in New Delhi has manufactured demons to comply with a narrow political agenda. Its search for a golden past requires changing names of streets, and identifying, abusing and occasionally lynching the conjured enemy. Pakistan has been through this motion in the past. That’s when schoolchildren were given controversial ideas about non-Muslims. An instructive moment came when a Muslim journalist from India who accompanied Atal Bihari Vajpayee on his visit to Pakistan in 1978 went with his colleagues to meet his cousins. At the emotional meeting, they also wanted to know discreetly if K.K. Katyal, Raghu Rai and Sumit Chakravarty were Hindu. “But they are just like us,” one cousin reportedly observed after being told of their Hindu identities. Today many centres in Pakistan are exploring and retrieving old names of their neighbourhoods with a view to restoring their Hindu or other non-Muslim identity. India, with the advent of Narendra Modi, is heading in the opposite direction. Mughal rule is being airbrushed from school curriculum. If more Indians could travel to Pakistan they would be able to see things similar to what I saw. A few days before the Lahore summit, I travelled with Sushma Swaraj and K.R. Malkani to the fabled Katas Raj Temple abutting the Lahore-Islamabad motorway. Malkani, an atheist, stood there looking amused as Swaraj dipped her hands into the sacred pond thought to have been used by the Pandavas during their exile. The caring way this temple and countless others have been preserved for Indian tourists will make more sense when people travel across the borders. This is not to say that minorities don’t face prejudice in Pakistan. Pakistani human rights activists have spoken strongly against forcible marriage of Hindu girls. The government has made some laws to deter the phenomenon but its impact is not uniformly felt. The prevalent bigotry on the Indian side finds state support often enough as it assumes the form of homes,mosquesand churches being vandalised or bulldozed accompanied by the occasional lynching of individuals from minorities. There seems to be a competition between bigots from both sides. At the SCO dialogue, a two-day session will centre on civilisational and cultural expression, art and architecture, language and literature, and religious and philosophical traditions. Delegates will also deliberate on filing joint multinational nominations for Unesco World Heritage recognition based on centuries of shared cultural exchange. Much of this will be problematic for the current ruling dispensation in India. In 2015, it had dubiously rejected a Unesco plan to declare Delhi a World Heritage City encompassing Old Delhi with its Mughal-era icons and British-era Lutyens’ New Delhi. To conclude, a telling story from the Maldives where Muslim zealots set fire to a Pakistani pavilion during a 2011 Saarc event and India watched the mayhem without a word of camaraderie with Pakistan. The event involved a display of national cultural treasures by Saarc states. Pakistan showcased its Buddhist heritage with tableaux of relics from Moenjodaro’s Indus civilisation. Extremists set fire to the Pakistan pavilion. The SCO dialogue offers as good an occasion as any to make amends to this witless aloofness between the two. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Peace prognosis
articles.content: AFGHAN foreign and domestic policies are a curious mix of tribalism, revanchism and ideological confusion thatshun human rightsand statecraft in favour of support for terrorist groups based on Afghan soil that pose a clear danger to regional peace. Unfortunately, all attempts at positive engagement with the Afghan Taliban by Pakistan as well as regional countries have been scuttled due to Kabul’s lack of willingness to rein in terrorist outfits operating under its benign gaze. A belief has gained traction amongst the Afghan Taliban that their successful armed struggle against Nato/USA could also be emulated by their ideological comrades like Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM, the TTP etc in pursuit of their political objectives. Rooted in medieval notions of tribal honour and revenge, the regime offers a propitious environment for growth of terror networks. The flow of external funds into the Afghan regime’s coffers has encouraged the obduracy of the Taliban, which continues channelling these funds to its ideological allies, sustaining the vicious cycle of terrorism and crime. Afghanistan is acting as a generous host for terrorist outfits that use its soil to generate economic rents through narco-trafficking, ransom, and smuggling. These groups are confident that their base of operation and sources of income would remain protected under the Taliban. A mere look at the figures showing the funding of this terror haven by the unsuspecting international community indicates why Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remains a threat. Since August 2021, donors have confirmed paying $8 billion in humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan through various international organisations, with a further $3.78bn committed and $94 million pledged. Billions more were reportedly received by the Taliban regime in direct foreign grants. Western capitals remain the biggest financial contributors to Afghanistan. The Afghan economy is kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking. Afghanistan imports goods worth around $12bn annually against exports of only $1.7bn, leaving an annual trade deficit of $10.3bn. It is intriguing how the Taliban regime is bridging $10.3bn every year. The answer lies in $17.5bn in foreign grants received since 2021, besides billions of dollars earned through narco-trafficking. It is clear evidence of an economy kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking. But the biggest question is: should such a regime that hosts terrorist groups be kept afloat through the largesse of international donors who might soon feel the heat from violent groups based in Afghanistan? If the international community thinks it can wean the Afghan Taliban away from terrorists, it needs to have a look at Pakistan’s 17 sincere attempts through ministers, the national security advisor, special representative, and joint coordination committee interactions, besides internationally mediated parleys in Doha, Istanbul, Riyadh and Urumqi. The reason for Afghan obstinacy is hubris and ideological narcissism that are pampered through foreign indulgence, despite zero concessions by the Kandahar-based ruling clique on political inclusivity, women’s education and minority rights. Pakistan has tried bilateral channels and has exhausted relevant regional fora like the trilateral group (Pakistan, China and Afghanistan) where in 2023 the Afghan foreign minister agreed to stop the flow of terrorism from Afghan soil. TheMoscow Format, which evolved out of a quadrilateral forum which was abandoned by the US after the Ukraine War, kept pressing the Afghan regime to abide by international counterterrorism obligations till its seventh meeting. However, it failed to elicit a positive response from the Taliban delegation during its eighth iteration at Moscow on Oct 5. The Taliban’s reluctance to even acknowledge the need to stop the activities of terrorist groups from Afghan soil betrays a mindset that is sympathetic to these violent groups. This should be a clear message to countries like Russia that are giving space to the Taliban regime in pursuit of narrow security goals. The fact is that all development and connectivity goals like TAPI, Casa-1000, and Trans-Afghan Railway, as well as mines and mineral exploration in Afghanistan, would remain a pipe dream till the time the Afghan Taliban stop sponsoring terrorism. The proceeds from illegal mining go to support the Taliban’s military infrastructure. Moreover, since 2021, it has established thousands of madressahs against 269 modern schools, replaced 90,000 teachers with around 100,000 Taliban-aligned clerics, abolished 18 university disciplines, rewritten 200-plus subjects and banned 679 textbooks. Until the Taliban regime gives up its support for terrorism and provides verifiable guarantees to Pakistan, meaningful normalisation, regional connectivity and lasting stability will not materialise.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Rabies elimination
articles.content: IT begins with a fever, a headache and a restlessness that will not settle. Then the patient panics at the sight of water. After days of going from hospital to hospital, the family learns that a dog bite weeks or months earlier, long healed and forgotten, carried rabies. The virus has reached the brain, and there is no cure. This scene plays out in hospitals across Pakistan every week, yet every such death is preventable. Sindh, where reporting has improved, recorded 285,000 dog bites in 2025 and over 200,000 by September 2026, with at least 41 rabies deaths this year. The Indus Hospital also saw rabies cases from Balochistan, and eight more came through teleconsultation from across the country. Punjab reported more than 1.3 million dog-bite cases between 2021 and March 2026. Estimates put Pakistan’s rabies deaths at 2,000 to 5,000 a year, most of them poor and many of them children. A study published this year in eBioMedicine, a Lancet journal, which I co-authored with Indus Hospital and Erasmus MC colleagues, shows how widely the virus circulates. We found rabies virus in 64 of 100 severe dog-bite wounds in Karachi, and two-thirds of the patients were children. It covered only severe bites, so it does not mean two in three biting dogs are rabid, but the warning is stark. If this is the picture in a city with the province’s best-equipped bite clinics, it is unlikely to be better elsewhere in Sindh or Pakistan. Elimination needs action on five fronts. The first is surveillance. Behind every reported case is a grieving family. Much of the recent rise reflects improved surveillance, and the true burden is still hidden. Many families believe the patient is possessed and turn to a shrine, not a hospital; others die in hospital undiagnosed. Surveillance must keep improving, with human rabies and dog bites notifiable at every level, so that reliable data reveals the true burden and where to focus resources. Swabbing bite wounds can also track the virus without catching dogs. Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility. The second is awareness. Children, especially boys, often tease street dogs and cannot defend themselves when attacked; peaceful coexistence starts with how we treat community dogs. Every household should know to wash a bite wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then seek immediate treatment at an anti-rabies centre, since washing reduces the virus but does not remove it. These messages belong in school curricula, mosques and the media. The third is correct treatment. Rabies is almost 100 per cent preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, and in our study nearly 96pc of patients developed protective antibodies. Yet roughly half of the rabies deaths reported at our centres occur in people whose treatment was incomplete or wrongly given. Immunoglobulin remains scarce, and too many patients drop out before finishing the course. Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility, and every doctor and nurse treating bites must be trained to WHO guidelines. The Sindh government’s ongoing rabies campaign deserves credit and, if sustained, can save many lives. The fourth is mass dog vaccination, because treating people alone will never end rabies. When at least 70pc of dogs are vaccinated year after year, the virus stops circulating. In September 2026, WHO validated Bhutan as the first country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted human rabies. The fifth is effective dog population management. Uncollected garbage feeds street dogs, which is why katchi abadis have the most dogs and the most bites. Views differ on the best methods, but any approach must be humane, guided by evidence and international standards, sustained over time, and backed by proper waste management and responsible ownership. Local governments, veterinary services and communities must agree on what works locally and monitor results. None of this can succeed in isolation. Health, livestock, local government and education departments each hold a piece and must work together under the One Health approach. The federal health minister’s in-principle approval of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework in July 2026 offers real hope. With timely notification, sustained funding and clear, measurable targets, it could become the turning point Pakistan has long awaited, with the media and civil society holding every institution to account. The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030. Bhutan has shown it can be done. A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now. The writer is technical lead, Rabies Prevention, Management & Training Services at the Indus Hospital & Health Network, Pakistan, and part of the National & Provincial Technical Working Advisory Group on Rabies.
articles.author: Muhammad Aftab Gohar

articles.title: Raised temperatures
articles.content: IT seems one of the government’s main coalition partners is becoming increasingly apprehensive about the measures being used to muzzle dissent. In a recent phone call with JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari stronglycondemned“the government’s actions and political vengeance” targeting the maulana’s party. He reportedly chided the government for being intolerant of criticism, while acknowledging that the opposition plays an “extremely important role in democracy and the parliamentary system”. During the conversation, he is also said to have expressed the view that the government should “refrain from such actions that weaken democracy and parliament.” The PPP chairman, it seems, wants to distance his party from the policies of the ruling PML-N. In recent weeks, he has urged his coalition partners to adopt a more conciliatory approach towards opposition parties andseek a national political reset. More cynical observers will describe this as buyer’s remorse. After all, one of the main reasons for the JUI-F’s discontent is the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. The order to impose those was signed, of course, by the co-chairperson of the PPP, President Asif Ali Zardari, despite many warnings that it would only complicate the country’s political crisis. Ever since he took an adversarial stance on the matter — a position precipitated by the government scuttling his efforts to mediate between it and the opposition parties — Mr Rehman has suddenly run into several ‘difficulties’. He has alleged that drones have been hovering over his home, and that his sons and other party leaders are being harassed by NAB. Several JUI-F leaders have also become the subject of smear videos online. His party is now taking to the streets to protest. The opposition is not an inconvenience to be managed, as Mr Bhutto-Zardari rightly pointed out. It is integral to the parliamentary system. When politicians suddenly face accountability after running into political disputes, questions arise about institutional credibility. The government, too, loses the moral authority it needs to rally the country against real threats. KP remains in the grip of a militant surge, and the federal government had justified its takeover of the province with the promise that it would stabilise it. The last thing that province needs is a fresh front of agitation, with yet another party on the streets while the security forces are under constant attack. What the country needs is for political temperatures to come down. The government should end its pressure tactics and open channels to the opposition. Disputes between political parties must be settled in parliament and at the negotiating table, not on the streets.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Water crisis
articles.content: PUNJAB’S looming water crisis should serve as a wake-up call for both federal and provincial policymakers. A new assessment by the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation warns that water demand in the province already exceeds supply across all sectors. Even more alarming is the annual depletion of 5.5bn cubic metres of groundwater. The province needs an additional 10bn cubic metres of usable water every year to bridge the supply-demand gap and sustain its aquifer. This shows the consequences of years of neglect and an approach to water management that has placed little emphasis on conservation. The FAO findings are based on water accounts covering 2012-17 but the trends hold. Punjab’s agricultural economy, expanding cities and growing population are placing increasing pressure on a resource that is already under severe stress. Agriculture, which accounts for the bulk of freshwater use, must be central to any serious conservation strategy. Much of Punjab still relies on traditional flood irrigation, an inefficient method that results in substantial losses. There is an urgent need to encourage a transition towards water-efficient technologies. This can help farmers produce more with less water. Crop choices also need to reflect local water availability. Furthermore, there is a case for developing smaller, distributed water storage facilities along riverbeds and suitable locations in the riverine belt. Such reservoirs, including off-channel storage and recharge ponds where feasible, could capture surplus flows during periods of high availability for use when supplies fall. This would offer a complementary and potentially cheaper option to large dams, whose construction involves substantial financial, environmental and social costs. Much of the rain that cities receive is channelled into drainage and sewerage systems due to rapid construction and the spread of concrete. Better urban planning must make rainwater harvesting, permeable surfaces, recharge wells and retention ponds integral to new housing schemes and public infrastructure. Cities need investment in systems that capture and store rainwater. Wastewater treatment and reuse, too, should become part of the province’s water strategy. The FAO’s proposal for a provincial water commission similarly deserves serious consideration.
articles.author: Editorial
